title: Rethinking Java Performance Analysis
problem: Java performance benchmarks and evaluation methodologies have drifted out of alignment with modern workloads and system behavior, undermining the reliability of empirical performance research built on them. Maintaining representative benchmarks and sound methodologies is difficult given the pace of language and system evolution.
motivation: Much systems innovation is grounded in performance analysis using benchmarks like DaCapo; if those benchmarks are unrepresentative or methodology is unsound, conclusions drawn from them may not generalize or reproduce.
method: The paper examines existing Java performance benchmarks and testing methods to find where they diverge from how real Java applications perform. It identifies three key problems: warm-up time (when Java's runtime translates and optimizes code at startup), just-in-time compilation artifacts (unexpected performance variations from the translation process itself), and measurement mistakes common in managed languages with automatic garbage collection. It then proposes better testing guidelines and practices that accurately reflect real-world Java performance.
key_novelty: Java's runtime features (just-in-time compilation and garbage collection) create measurement artifacts that invalidate standard performance testing practices.
contributions: Critical analysis of representativeness of current Java benchmarks (e.g., DaCapo) vs. modern workloads
Identification of methodological pitfalls in Java performance evaluation (warm-up, JIT, GC interactions)
Proposed guidelines and principles for more principled Java performance analysis
Lessons drawn that generalize to other managed languages and performance-analysis fields

metrics.other: methodology critique; no single headline number

limitations: Prescriptive methodology improvements are not yet validated with a new benchmark suite in this paper.
primary_theme: methodological soundness of Java performance benchmarking
